case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a property owner may sue a State directly under the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause for just compensation (i.e., bring a “complete” takings claim) when no legislatively created cause of action is invoked, or whether such claims must proceed only via a statutory vehicle such as 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Takings Clause, applied to States via the Fourteenth Amendment); 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (as the disputed statutory vehicle for a federal takings remedy); related background issue: state sovereign immunity/waiver principles.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue the Fifth Circuit wrongly held that property owners lack any freestanding federal right of action to obtain just compensation for a taking and therefore cannot bring a complete Takings Clause claim in state or federal court absent a legislatively created remedy (like § 1983). They contend this rule conflicts with decisions from other courts, and that Knick does not resolve the distinct question whether the Constitution itself supplies a cause of action/remedy. They also argue Texas’s asserted alternative grounds (e.g., sovereign immunity bars damages) are not a vehicle problem for Supreme Court review because the Fifth Circuit did not address them and the Court can remand for consideration; in any event, petitioners point to Texas authorities indicating takings claims waive immunity from suit for compensation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Texas argues that, as the Fifth Circuit held, the Takings Clause does not itself create a standalone cause of action for damages; absent a legislatively provided remedy (and in practice outside § 1983), property owners cannot bring a complete federal takings claim. In opposing certiorari, Texas further suggests it would inevitably prevail on alternative legal grounds (including sovereign-immunity-based arguments that would bar damages even if the case proceeds), implying the case is a poor vehicle for deciding the question presented.
key_precedents: First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles (1987)
Zito v. N.C. Coastal Resources Comm’n (4th Cir. 2021), cert. denied, 142 S. Ct. 465 (2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s core point—that a money-mandating constitutional duty does not automatically entail a freestanding damages cause of action against a State in the face of sovereign immunity—is the strongest argument on the other side, and we should not decide more than necessary. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Jacobs and First English describe the Just Compensation Clause as “self-executing” and “of its own force,” which is difficult to square with a rule that the constitutional obligation can be nullified by the absence of a statutory vehicle. Knick’s statement that the claim is “complete” at the time of the taking reinforces that the Constitution supplies the compensation entitlement independent of legislative grace, even if sovereign-immunity and proper-forum/defendant questions constrain enforcement. The narrow, legitimacy-protecting course is to recognize the existence of the constitutional compensation claim while remanding unresolved immunity/vehicle issues rather than implying a broad new remedial regime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is the remedial-vehicle/sovereign-immunity distinction: the Takings Clause does not spell out a named defendant, forum, or procedural mechanism. But the original public meaning of “nor shall … be taken … without just compensation” is a money-mandating limitation on government power that is violated at the moment of uncompensated taking, and as the Chief Justice notes, Jacobs and First English treat that obligation as enforceable “of its own force,” not dependent on legislative grace. Sovereign immunity may constrain the particular defendant or forum, but it cannot be used to recharacterize the Clause as merely aspirational or to make the existence of the constitutional claim turn on § 1983’s availability—an inversion of the Constitution–statute hierarchy. I therefore agree with Justice Gorsuch and the Chief that we can recognize the constitutional compensation claim while leaving immunity/vehicle issues for remand or narrower resolution.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Jacobs/First English/Knick persuades me that the compensation obligation arises immediately “of its own force,” but that still does not answer the distinct remedial question whether the Fifth Amendment itself implies a freestanding damages cause of action against a State notwithstanding sovereign-immunity and our usual cause-of-action principles. Jacobs involved the federal government in a setting with established money-mandating remedial avenues; it does not compel the inference that the Constitution silently authorizes suits for damages against States without a statutory vehicle. Textually, the Clause mandates that compensation be provided, but it is silent on who may be sued and in what forum—questions our doctrine generally treats as governed by background immunity rules and legislatively supplied vehicles like § 1983 or state inverse-condemnation procedures. I therefore do not think Knick’s “claim is complete” language can be transmuted into a constitutional damages action that would destabilize settled immunity and remedial doctrine.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s distinction between a money-mandating constitutional duty and a freestanding damages cause of action is the best point for the Respondent, because sovereign-immunity background rules can constrain whom a plaintiff may sue and in what forum. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Jacobs and First English describe the Just Compensation Clause as operating “of its own force,” and Knick’s “complete” claim framing is hard to square with a regime where compensation depends on legislative remedial happenstance that can, in practice, leave ordinary property owners without a judicial path. I agree with Justice Kavanaugh’s institutional approach: we can recognize a constitutional compensation claim while leaving the immunity/vehicle and proper-defendant questions to remand, rather than converting those downstream limits into a categorical denial of enforceability. Pragmatically, denying a direct constitutional basis would predictably close courthouse doors to less-resourced claimants and undermine the Clause’s fairness function, even if the State ultimately prevails on immunity in a particular forum.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s remedial-vehicle/sovereign-immunity point is the hardest: calling the Clause “self-executing” might speak only to when the duty arises, not to an all-purpose damages action against a State. But Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s narrower framing persuades me that we can (and should) recognize, on the text (“without just compensation”) and our money-mandating language in Jacobs and First English, that a taking yields a complete constitutional entitlement to compensation “of its own force,” without deciding the full suite of forum/defendant/immunity mechanics. Knick’s insistence that the claim is “complete” at the time of the taking makes it pragmatically incoherent to condition the very existence of the constitutional claim on the happenstance of § 1983 or state remedial design. Sovereign immunity may still constrain who can be sued and where, but under my textualist/pragmatic approach that downstream limitation cannot be converted into a categorical denial that the Constitution itself supplies an enforceable compensation obligation once a taking is shown.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s remedial-vehicle point usefully separates (1) the existence of a constitutional entitlement from (2) the forum and defendant against whom it may be enforced, but it does not defeat the money-mandating command of the Takings Clause itself (“without just compensation”). As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, Jacobs and First English describe the Clause as “self-executing” and operating “of its own force,” and Knick’s statement that the claim is “complete” at the time of the taking is difficult to square with making judicial enforceability contingent on a statute Congress or a State may withhold. On a textualist and separation-of-powers view, we should not adopt a rule that effectively allows legislatures to decide whether an express constitutional compensation mandate is judicially cognizable at all. I agree with Justice Roberts that we can hold narrowly that the Fifth Amendment supplies a complete compensation claim upon a taking while leaving sovereign-immunity/proper-defendant questions for remand rather than announcing a sweeping new damages regime.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains the remedial-vehicle/sovereign-immunity distinction: “self-executing” could be read to establish only a substantive duty, not a freestanding damages action against a State. But Chief Justice Roberts persuasively grounds our narrower path in Jacobs and First English, which describe the Just Compensation Clause as money-mandating “of its own force,” and Knick’s statement that the claim is “complete” at the time of the taking is hard to square with a rule that no judicially cognizable claim exists absent § 1983 or state legislative permission. Under an institutionalist, precedent-focused approach, we can recognize the constitutional compensation claim while reserving Alito’s forum/defendant/immunity concerns for remand—avoiding an unnecessary upheaval of sovereign-immunity doctrine yet preserving the Constitution’s mandatory command. Nothing Justice Alito identifies squarely undermines that limited holding, because his concern goes to who may be sued and where, not whether the Fifth Amendment itself supplies an enforceable compensation obligation once a taking is established.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that “self-executing” may speak only to the existence/timing of the compensation duty, not to a freestanding damages cause of action against a State in the face of sovereign-immunity background rules—does not overcome the textual and precedential evidence that the Just Compensation Clause is money-mandating and judicially enforceable “of its own force.” As the Chief Justice emphasizes, making the existence of a complete constitutional right depend on a legislatively supplied vehicle like § 1983 risks permitting States (or Congress) to defeat an express constitutional command through remedial design, in tension with Knick’s understanding that the claim is “complete” when the taking occurs. Jacobs and First English, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, use “self-executing” in a way that supports a court’s authority to award compensation once a taking is established, even if sovereign immunity still constrains the proper defendant, forum, or form of relief. I therefore maintain that the Constitution supplies a cognizable compensation claim, while agreeing with Roberts that the sovereign-immunity/vehicle questions can be handled narrowly and, to the extent not resolved below, on remand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s remedial-vehicle point remains the most serious: “self-executing” could be read as describing only a substantive duty, leaving the cause-of-action/forum question to background immunity and legislative design. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rightly emphasize that Jacobs and First English treat the Just Compensation Clause as money-mandating “of its own force,” and Knick’s “complete at the time of the taking” framing makes it pragmatically and procedurally unfair to condition a fully accrued constitutional violation on statutory happenstance like § 1983. I agree sovereign-immunity and proper-defendant limits may still narrow who can be sued and where, yet those downstream constraints do not justify a categorical rule that the Fifth Amendment can never itself supply the basis for seeking compensation. On my methodology, recognizing the constitutional claim while leaving immunity/vehicle issues for remand best preserves doctrinal coherence and real-world enforceability without gratuitously expanding remedies beyond what the case requires.

John Roberts.reasoning: This Court has repeatedly described the Takings Clause’s just-compensation requirement as “self-executing,” which strongly suggests that, once a taking is shown, the Constitution itself supplies a mandatory compensation remedy rather than leaving the availability of compensation to legislative grace. See First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304, 315–16 (1987); Knick v. Township of Scott, 139 S. Ct. 2162, 2172 (2019). Requiring property owners to identify a separate legislatively created cause of action as a prerequisite to a “complete” Takings Clause claim risks undermining the Clause’s remedial command and invites States to defeat federal rights by remedial design, a result difficult to square with our takings cases. Any sovereign-immunity or vehicle objections Texas raises were not passed upon below and can be addressed on remand, allowing a narrow holding limited to the existence of a constitutional compensation claim without deciding the full scope of remedies or forum.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text—“nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation”—is best read as a self-executing constitutional command that itself supplies both the right and the remedial entitlement to compensation when a taking occurs, rather than a mere hortatory principle dependent on legislative grace. This Court has repeatedly treated just compensation as constitutionally required and judicially enforceable (Jacobs v. United States, 290 U.S. 13 (1933); First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304, 315–16 (1987)), and Knick v. Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180 (2019), confirms that a takings claim is “complete” when the taking happens, not only after a state provides a statutory remedy. Nothing in 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suggests Congress made it the exclusive vehicle for vindicating takings rights, and a rule requiring § 1983 would improperly allow States to defeat an express constitutional compensation mandate by withholding a cause of action. Any state sovereign-immunity complications are separate from the question presented and can be addressed on remand, but they do not justify denying that the Constitution itself creates an enforceable right to compensation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Takings Clause establishes a substantive constitutional entitlement to just compensation, but it does not, by its own terms, prescribe a freestanding cause of action against a State in the absence of a legislatively created remedial vehicle. Whatever broad language appears in First English about the compensation requirement being “self-executing,” that does not resolve the distinct question presented here—whether a plaintiff may sue a State directly for damages without proceeding under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 or some comparable statutory authorization, particularly given background doctrines of sovereign immunity. Knick confirms when a takings claim accrues and rejects state-litigation exhaustion, but it does not hold that the Constitution itself supplies a universal damages cause of action against States. As a practical matter, treating the Takings Clause as an implied, general damages action would invite substantial disruption of established remedial and immunity frameworks, and Congress has already provided a principal vehicle in § 1983 for constitutional claims against state actors.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Takings Clause is uniquely remedial in text—"nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation"—and this Court has repeatedly described compensation claims as "grounded in the Constitution itself." First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles held the Constitution requires a compensation remedy when a taking occurs, and Knick reiterated that a taking without compensation violates the "self-executing" Fifth Amendment at the time of the taking. Requiring owners to locate a separate legislatively created cause of action as a precondition to any "complete" takings claim risks leaving some property owners—especially individuals and small businesses—without a practical avenue for compensation, undermining fairness and access to justice. Section 1983 may often provide a vehicle, but it should not be treated as the exclusive gateway for enforcing a constitutional command that specifies its own remedy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Takings Clause is textually distinct in that it both prohibits uncompensated takings and specifies the remedy—“just compensation”—making it plausibly self-executing as to the government’s duty to pay once a taking occurs. This Court has repeatedly treated compensation as constitutionally required “of its own force,” see First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304, 316 n.9 (1987), and Knick v. Township of Scott, 139 S. Ct. 2162, 2172 (2019), which supports allowing a “complete” takings claim without hinging enforceability on a legislatively created cause of action like 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Requiring § 1983 as the exclusive vehicle would create serious workability and coherence problems (including making constitutional compensation depend on statutory happenstance) and risks reviving procedural traps Knick sought to eliminate. Texas’s sovereign-immunity arguments may affect the proper forum or remedy and can be addressed on remand, but they do not justify a categorical rule that the Constitution provides no direct basis for seeking just compensation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment’s text supplies both the right and the remedy: if property is taken “for public use,” it must be accompanied by “just compensation,” and this Court has long described that compensation obligation as constitutionally required upon the taking. First English explained that the Just Compensation Clause “of its own force furnish[es] a basis for a court to award money damages against the government,” and Knick reaffirmed that the right to compensation vests “immediately upon a taking,” which is hard to square with a rule that no judicial remedy exists absent a legislative cause of action like 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Treating § 1983 as the exclusive vehicle would improperly shift to Congress the power to decide whether a constitutional command is judicially enforceable, raising separation-of-powers concerns and weakening a textual constitutional guarantee. Any sovereign-immunity limits on the forum or the proper defendant are distinct questions from whether the Takings Clause itself is self-executing as to the compensation remedy, and can be addressed on remand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Takings Clause has long been understood as “self-executing” as to the obligation to pay just compensation, and this Court has stated that it “of its own force furnish[es] a basis for a court to award money damages against the government.” First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304, 316 n.9 (1987) (quoting Jacobs v. United States, 290 U.S. 13, 16 (1933)). Knick v. Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180 (2019), reinforces that the right to compensation vests immediately upon a taking, which is difficult to square with a rule that no “complete” federal claim exists absent a statutory cause of action. While § 1983 is a common vehicle, it should not be treated as the exclusive path if the constitutional right itself historically supports a judicial remedy; any sovereign-immunity/waiver questions can be addressed on remand under ordinary precedent and workability considerations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text (“nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation”) is best read, in its original public meaning, as imposing an immediately enforceable duty to pay when a taking occurs, not a duty contingent on legislative grace. Our cases describe that compensation obligation as “self-executing” with respect to the remedy, explaining that the right to recover “rest[s] upon the Fifth Amendment” and needs no “statutory recognition,” Jacobs v. United States, 290 U.S. 13, 16 (1933), a principle reiterated in First English Evangelical Lutheran Church v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304, 316 (1987), and relied upon in Knick v. Township of Scott, 139 S. Ct. 2162, 2171 (2019). Section 1983 may provide a familiar vehicle against appropriate defendants, but nothing in § 1983’s text purports to make it the exclusive means to vindicate the Constitution’s own money-mandating command. To the extent state sovereign-immunity defenses bear on the forum or defendant, that is a distinct question from whether the Constitution itself supplies a complete claim for just compensation, and it does not justify denying the existence of the constitutional cause of action.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Takings Clause is unusual among constitutional guarantees because it specifies the remedy as part of the right: when the government takes property, it "must" provide just compensation, and this Court has described compensation as constitutionally required rather than merely a legislatively supplied benefit. In First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, the Court emphasized that just-compensation claims are "grounded in the Constitution itself" and that the Clause can “of its own force furnish a basis for a court to award money damages,” which strongly supports allowing a complete takings claim without making § 1983 the exclusive vehicle. Knick v. Township of Scott further reinforces that the right to compensation vests immediately upon a taking, making it procedurally unfair to deny any judicial forum absent a statutory cause of action. Whether Texas can ultimately invoke sovereign-immunity limits is a distinct question better addressed on remand, but it should not justify a categorical rule that the Fifth Amendment never supplies a direct basis to seek just compensation.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause is self-executing such that property owners may sue a State directly for just compensation in the absence of a legislatively created cause of action (and not solely via 42 U.S.C. § 1983).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Takings Clause), as incorporated against the States via the Fourteenth Amendment; related remedial vehicle: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (as debated in the briefs).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Fifth Circuit incorrectly held there is no freestanding federal right to bring a Takings Clause claim unless a legislature has provided a cause of action (e.g., through § 1983). They contend the Takings Clause itself requires compensation when property is taken, making the compensation remedy directly enforceable in court (i.e., the Clause is self-executing), and they emphasize a recognized split among courts nationwide on whether a takings plaintiff must proceed via § 1983 or can sue directly under the Constitution. Petitioners also argue there is no 'vehicle' problem: Texas’s alternative defenses (e.g., sovereign immunity arguments after removal) were rejected by the district court and not addressed by the Fifth Circuit, so the Supreme Court can resolve the remedial question and leave other issues for remand.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Texas argues the petition should be denied because the Fifth Circuit’s approach is correct: absent a legislatively created remedy, property owners cannot bring a complete Takings Clause claim directly under the Constitution, and § 1983 is the exclusive (or necessary) vehicle for enforcing federal takings rights in court. In the alternative, Texas suggests that even if the Court took the case, Texas would ultimately prevail on other grounds (framed as 'vehicle' problems), including arguments tied to sovereign immunity and limits on damages—asserting those defenses would bar recovery even if the takings theory were otherwise viable.
key_precedents: Knick v. Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180 (2019)
First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304 (1987)
Zito v. N.C. Coastal Resources Commission, 8 F.4th 281 (4th Cir. 2021), cert. denied, 142 S. Ct. 465 (2021)
City of Baytown v. Schrock, 645 S.W.3d 174 (Tex. 2022)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—separation of powers and the need for an express statutory cause of action to obtain money damages—has force in the Bivens context, but it fits poorly with the Takings Clause’s text, which is itself money-mandating (“without just compensation”). As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, our precedents describing the Clause as “self-executing” (Jacobs; First English) are best read not as open-ended remedial invention but as recognition that a completed taking gives rise to an immediately accrued constitutional entitlement to compensation. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Jacobs strengthens the narrow ground: we can reject the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule while leaving sovereign-immunity, proper-defendant, and forum/vehicle issues to be addressed on remand. That minimalist disposition respects precedent and institutional legitimacy without deciding more than necessary about § 1983 exclusivity or immunity waivers.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—separation of powers and sovereign immunity—assumes that a damages remedy must come from legislative grace, but the Takings Clause’s text (“without just compensation”) is itself money-mandating and thus supplies the rule of decision at the moment of the taking. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow approach is consistent with an original public-meaning reading: recognize that the constitutional obligation to pay is self-executing (as Jacobs and First English say) without deciding in this posture which vehicle, forum, or defendant ultimately permits collection. Justice Barrett is right that this is not a Bivens-style implied cause of action; it is enforcement of an express constitutional condition on governmental power, and Knick’s immediacy principle confirms the claim is complete when the taking occurs. Because § 1983 contains no textual exclusivity and cannot be read to nullify a constitutional payment command, the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule cannot stand, though immunity and forum limits remain for remand.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—separation of powers and the usual reluctance to infer damages actions absent a statutory vehicle—has force in the Bivens context, but it does not fit the Takings Clause’s text, which conditions the legitimacy of a taking on payment of “just compensation.” Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach is the right way to respect those institutional concerns: recognize that the Constitution is money-mandating and that a plaintiff states a federal claim at the moment of a completed taking, while leaving sovereign-immunity, proper-defendant, and forum questions for remand. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Jacobs and First English strengthens the conclusion that this is not judicial “remedial invention” but enforcement of an obligation the Constitution itself imposes “of its own force.” On a textualist account attentive to practical consequences, the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule would risk turning an express constitutional payment command into legislative grace, without any convincing constitutional or precedential basis to do so.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s separation-of-powers point—that damages require an express statutory cause of action—has force in the ordinary implied-remedy context, but it weakens substantially where the Constitution itself is money-mandating and expressly conditions the taking power on payment. Justice Kagan’s framing is decisive for me: treating § 1983 (or any statute) as an exclusive gatekeeper would convert an immediate constitutional entitlement into remedial grace and create procedural gaps that predictably burden less-resourced property owners. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Jacobs and the Chief Justice’s emphasis on a narrow holding, together with First English and Knick’s “of its own force” and immediacy principles, confirm that the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule cannot stand even if sovereign immunity and proper-defendant issues remain for remand. Those downstream limits can be litigated without denying the existence of the constitutional claim itself, which is what risks leaving real people uncompensated for an admitted taking.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best separation-of-powers point—that courts should not infer damages actions absent congressional authorization and that § 1983 is the intended vehicle—has force in the ordinary implied-remedy setting, but it fits the Takings Clause poorly because the text itself couples the taking with an express payment command (“without just compensation”), making the obligation money-mandating rather than judicially invented. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach most appeals to my pragmatic textualism: reverse the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule while reserving sovereign immunity, proper defendant, and forum/vehicle issues for remand, which preserves workable boundaries without converting the constitutional entitlement into legislative grace. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Jacobs, and Justice Barrett’s emphasis on the Clause’s “self-executing” character, strengthens the conclusion that our precedents treat the compensation duty as enforceable “of its own force,” consistent with First English and Knick’s immediacy principle. I therefore do not see a separation-of-powers objection strong enough to justify a rule that a concededly complete constitutional taking yields no federal claim until Congress speaks.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—separation of powers and the need for a legislatively supplied cause of action for damages against a State—has force in ordinary implied-remedy cases, but it fits poorly with a clause that by its terms forbids a taking “without just compensation.” Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach is the right institutional answer: recognize that the Takings Clause is money-mandating and “self-executing” in the Jacobs/First English sense (a claim is complete at the taking, as Knick reinforces), while leaving sovereign-immunity, proper-defendant, and forum/vehicle issues for remand rather than collapsing them into a categorical no-cause-of-action rule. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on Jacobs is especially persuasive for an originalist: if the Constitution itself specifies compensation as the condition of lawful taking, courts are not “creating” a remedy in the Bivens sense so much as applying the rule of decision the text supplies. Requiring statutory grace as a prerequisite would risk converting an express constitutional payment obligation into something contingent, which our precedent has repeatedly rejected.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—separation of powers and sovereign immunity concerns about recognizing a damages action absent statutory authorization—does not defeat the threshold proposition that the Takings Clause itself is money-mandating and “self-executing.” Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach is institutionally sound: we can reject the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule by holding that a completed taking states a federal constitutional claim for just compensation, while leaving the forum/vehicle and immunity/defendant questions for remand. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Jacobs (and the Court’s repeated statements that compensation is due “without statutory recognition”) strengthens the historical and precedential footing, and it fits with First English and Knick’s immediacy principle that the right accrues at the time of the taking. Properly understood, recognizing the constitutional obligation does not itself create an unlimited judicial remedial regime; it simply prevents the constitutional duty from being reduced to legislative grace.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—separation of powers and sovereign-immunity concerns if we recognize a “direct” Takings Clause action—does not defeat the threshold issue whether the Constitution itself imposes an enforceable compensation obligation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the Clause is textually money-mandating (“without just compensation”), and Jacobs and First English describe the duty as arising “of its own force,” which is difficult to reconcile with the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule. Knick’s completion-at-the-taking principle further undercuts any theory that a legislature must first create a remedial vehicle before a constitutional claim exists, even if immunity and proper-defendant questions may limit where and against whom relief is available. I therefore agree with Justice Kagan’s proposed narrow disposition: recognize the self-executing federal claim while expressly leaving vehicle, forum, and sovereign-immunity issues for remand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest separation-of-powers point—that damages require an express statutory cause of action and courts should not infer one—has less traction here because the Takings Clause is uniquely money-mandating, and conditioning compensation on legislative grace risks remedial gaps inconsistent with procedural fairness. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow disposition is persuasive: recognize that a completed taking states a federal constitutional claim for just compensation while leaving the vehicle, forum, and sovereign-immunity questions for remand rather than using them to erase the entitlement at the threshold. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Jacobs (and the “self-executing” language echoed in First English) strengthens that this is not Bivens-style remedial invention but enforcement of an express constitutional payment obligation. Those immunity and defendant issues may still bar relief in a particular posture, but they are analytically distinct from the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Takings Clause is textually distinctive: it does not merely prohibit conduct but affirmatively specifies the remedy—“nor shall private property be taken … without just compensation”—and this Court has repeatedly treated the compensation obligation as arising immediately upon the taking. First English expressly recognized that the Just Compensation Clause “of its own force furnish[es] a basis for a court to award money damages against the government,” and Knick reaffirmed that a property owner’s right to compensation vests at the time of the taking, not after the State provides a remedial scheme. A narrow ruling can respect precedent and institutional legitimacy by holding only that a plaintiff states a federal claim for just compensation directly under the Takings Clause (as incorporated via the Fourteenth Amendment), leaving questions of sovereign immunity, removal, and the proper forum or remedy to be addressed on remand; § 1983 may be an available vehicle, but it is not the exclusive source of the right to seek compensation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text—“nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation”—is best read, as an original matter, to impose a judicially enforceable duty to pay compensation when the government takes property, not a mere aspiration contingent on legislative grace. This Court has repeatedly described the compensation requirement as “self-executing,” explaining that the constitutional right to recover just compensation “rests upon the Fifth Amendment” and needs no “statutory recognition,” Jacobs v. United States, 290 U.S. 13, 16 (1933), a principle reaffirmed in First English, 482 U.S. at 316, and echoed in Knick, 588 U.S. at 194. Section 1983 may provide a vehicle in many cases, but nothing in its text makes it the exclusive means of enforcing the Constitution, and the Fifth Circuit’s rule would improperly allow a State to evade a money-mandating constitutional command by withholding a cause of action. Because the Takings Clause itself supplies the substantive right and remedy of just compensation at the time of the taking, property owners may sue to vindicate that right even absent a legislatively created cause of action.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text provides its own remedial rule—private property shall not be taken “without just compensation”—and this Court has repeatedly described that compensation obligation as constitutionally required and judicially enforceable. In First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, the Court rejected the contention that the Constitution cannot “of its own force” support a money award and explained that the Just Compensation Clause itself “furnish[es] a basis for a court to award money damages against the government.” Knick v. Township of Scott likewise characterizes the Clause as “self-executing” and recognizes that the right to compensation accrues immediately upon a taking, undermining the Fifth Circuit’s premise that a legislature must create a cause of action before any federal takings claim exists. Section 1983 may be an available vehicle, but nothing in its text makes it exclusive for enforcing a self-executing constitutional compensation command; any distinct sovereign-immunity or remedial limitations can be addressed separately on remand.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Takings Clause is best understood as self-executing in the sense that, once a taking occurs, the Constitution itself supplies the entitlement to “just compensation,” not merely a right to seek prospective invalidation. In First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, the Court stated that “statutory recognition was not necessary” because just-compensation claims “are grounded in the Constitution itself,” and it rejected the view that the Constitution cannot “of its own force” support a court-ordered compensation remedy. Knick v. Township of Scott likewise confirms that a property owner’s claim is complete at the time of the taking and that the right to compensation vests immediately, undermining a rule that would condition access to a judicial remedy on a legislature’s creation of a cause of action. Given the practical stakes—ensuring meaningful access to compensation and preventing States from evading accountability through remedial gaps—I would reverse the Fifth Circuit’s categorical no-cause-of-action rule while leaving any distinct sovereign-immunity or procedural defenses for remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text is remedial in a way most constitutional provisions are not: it pairs the prohibition on uncompensated takings with an affirmative command—property “shall not… be taken… without just compensation,” U.S. Const. amend. V—supporting the view that the compensation obligation is judicially enforceable without further legislative authorization. This Court has repeatedly described the Just Compensation Clause as “self-executing,” explaining that a property owner’s right to compensation vests immediately upon a taking and that the Clause “of its own force furnish[es] a basis for a court to award money damages,” First English Evangelical Lutheran Church v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304, 316 & n.9 (1987); see also Knick v. Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180, 194–195 (2019). Requiring § 1983 as an exclusive vehicle would turn a constitutional remedy into a statutory grace and create unnecessary workability problems and incoherence across jurisdictions where § 1983 is unavailable or contested, contrary to Knick’s insistence on an actionable violation at the time of the taking. Texas’s alternative defenses (e.g., sovereign immunity/vehicle issues) may bear on ultimate relief, but they do not justify a categorical rule denying a direct constitutional cause of action where the Constitution itself specifies the compensation remedy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text is remedial as well as prohibitory: when property is taken for public use, the Constitution itself commands that “just compensation” be paid, and this Court has repeatedly described that obligation as self-executing. In First English, the Court rejected the view that the Constitution “does not, of its own force, furnish a basis for a court to award money damages against the government,” emphasizing that “it is the Constitution that dictates the remedy” for a taking. Knick likewise confirms that the right to compensation vests “immediately upon a taking,” and nothing in § 1983’s text makes it the exclusive vehicle for enforcing that constitutional command. Separation-of-powers principles counsel against requiring a statutory cause of action before a court may enforce an express constitutional payment obligation, though any distinct sovereign-immunity defenses remain for consideration on remand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Takings Clause is unusual in that it not only recognizes a right but also specifies the remedy—“just compensation”—and this Court has repeatedly described that remedial obligation as constitutionally compelled. In First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, the Court explained that the Just Compensation Clause “of its own force furnish[es] a basis for a court to award money damages against the government,” and Knick v. Township of Scott reiterated that a property owner’s right to compensation arises “immediately upon a taking” under the “self-executing” Fifth Amendment. Requiring a legislatively created cause of action as a categorical prerequisite would sit uneasily with that history and with the practical need for a workable, uniform federal remedy for constitutional takings. While Texas may raise sovereign-immunity or other defenses on remand, the constitutional question presented—whether the Takings Clause itself supplies an enforceable compensation remedy—should be answered yes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Takings Clause’s text—“nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation”—is best read as money-mandating and self-executing as to the compensation remedy, so that a property owner has a constitutional claim for just compensation at the time of the taking. This Court has long described the compensation obligation as arising directly from the Constitution “without statutory recognition,” Jacobs v. United States, 290 U.S. 13, 16 (1933), and Knick v. Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180 (2019), reaffirmed that “self-executing character” in holding that a takings claim is complete when the taking occurs. Section 1983 is a familiar vehicle to enforce federal rights, but nothing in its text makes it the exclusive means of vindicating the Takings Clause, and treating it as exclusive sits uneasily with the Clause’s original public meaning and this Court’s repeated statements that the Constitution itself supplies the right to compensation. Any distinct sovereign-immunity or remedial limits issues are analytically separate from whether the Takings Clause itself furnishes a direct claim for just compensation and can be addressed on remand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Takings Clause is best understood as self-executing as to the compensation obligation: it "of its own force" supplies the rule and basis for a court to award compensation once a taking has occurred, without requiring prior “statutory recognition,” as this Court stated in First English Evangelical Lutheran Church of Glendale v. County of Los Angeles, 482 U.S. 304, 315–16 & n.9 (1987). Knick v. Township of Scott, 588 U.S. 180 (2019), reinforces that the right to just compensation accrues immediately upon the taking, underscoring that procedural barriers should not deny a meaningful remedy for a completed constitutional violation. While 42 U.S.C. § 1983 is a common remedial vehicle against state and local officials, nothing in § 1983’s text makes it exclusive, and insisting on a legislatively created cause of action as a prerequisite risks arbitrary, unfair remedial gaps inconsistent with the practical consequences the Clause is designed to prevent. Any sovereign-immunity or remedial-limit defenses Texas may assert are distinct from the threshold question presented and can be addressed on remand without rewriting the constitutional remedial principle recognized in First English.
